antecedent

an-tih-SEE-dint -- from Latin ante- ('before') + cedere ('to go'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Antecedent is something that existed before and serves as the origin, cause, or reference point for something later.

Historians trace the antecedents of the modern labor movement back to small worker guilds in the 1800s.

Worked Example

Grammar teachers point out that in the sentence 'Maria lost her keys,' the word 'her' refers back to its antecedent, Maria.

Notice that the antecedent isn't just 'something old' -- it's specifically the earlier thing that the later thing depends on or refers back to, whether that's a pronoun's noun or a modern movement's historical roots.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

predecessor: A predecessor held the same job or slot immediately before -- the previous model, the outgoing mayor -- so the word is about position in a line. An antecedent is about influence: the earlier thing a later one grew from or refers back to, whatever slot it occupied.

ancestor: An ancestor sits generations back on a family line, and the word keeps that family flavor even for machines -- the abacus as the computer's ancestor. Antecedent is drier and more logical: the earlier origin or reference point, with no family metaphor attached.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

successor: something that follows and takes the place of another

descendant: something that developed later, out of an earlier source

Where it sits · how strongly it caused what followed — forerunner → antecedent → precursor

forerunner vs. antecedent: Forerunner is weaker than antecedent: calling the telegraph a forerunner only says it came earlier, while an antecedent makes the stronger claim of being the later thing's actual origin.

precursor vs. antecedent: Precursor goes further than antecedent: an antecedent is a reference point in the past, but calling clay tablets a precursor of the book claims they directly led to it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ante-

prefix — ante-: before (Latin)

root — -ced-

root — -ced-: to go, to yield (Latin (cedere))

suffix — -ent

suffix — -ent: one who or that which; forms a noun or adjective (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin ante- ('before') plus cedere ('to go') plus the suffix -ent, 'that which': literally 'that which goes before.' An antecedent is the earlier thing a later thing traces back to.

Use the root in a new word: precede

Use the root in a new word: precede: A short warning chime always precedes the train doors closing.

Root Check

Word Choice

Antecedent is about a logical or causal relationship -- what came before and helped shape what came after. Compare "bygone," which is about nostalgia for an earlier time with no claim about cause and effect, and "foregone," which describes an outcome that feels certain in advance, not something from the past at all.
